chapter_approach.heading: How this chapter is taught
chapter_approach.intro: The chapter follows the book's own order: fractals first, then solids. Each fractal is built one step at a time and its counts are predicted before they are revealed, so a picture becomes a rule (multiply by 8, multiply by 4). Solids are first pictured in the mind, then cut, unfolded, flattened onto a plane and finally drawn on an isometric grid.

points.title: Predict, then check
points.text: Each idea opens with a question answered before the reveal: how many squares at the next step, will this shape fold into a cube, is this path really the shortest.

points.title: Imagine before you handle
points.text: The book asks students to visualise first and only then use cutouts. The plan keeps that order: the video asks for a mental picture, and a tool appears only where handling the shape is the idea.

points.title: Tools only where manipulation is the concept
points.text: Ten tools, each used once: stepping three fractals, counting the parts of solids, folding and rolling nets, unfolding a box to find a path, tilting a solid to see its projection, turning a solid to read its views, and stacking cubes on an isometric grid. Topics about ideas carry no tool.

points.title: Many right answers
points.text: Profiles, projections and nets rarely have one answer. Students are asked for more than one solid that fits a view, and for every unfolding before choosing the shortest path.

modules.module_summary: Self-similar shapes in nature and in mathematics. The Sierpinski Carpet, the Sierpinski Triangle and the Koch Snowflake are built by repeating one rule; counting squares, holes, sides, area and perimeter step by step turns each picture into a pattern of numbers. Fractals in temples, blankets and prints close the module.

concepts.concept_name: A fern made of smaller ferns

content.text:
In this chapter, we will explore two geometric themes. We will study fractals which are self-similar shapes. They exhibit the same or similar pattern over and over again, but at smaller and smaller scales. We will then look at different ways of visualising solids.
4.1 Fractals
One of the most beautiful examples of a fractal that also occurs in nature is the fern. The fern is seen to have smaller copies of itself as its leaves, and these in turn have even smaller copies of themselves in their sub-leaves, and so on!
Similar phenomena of self-similarity occur in trees (where a trunk has limbs, and a limb has branches, and the branches have branchlets, and so on), clouds, coastlines, mountains, lightning, and many other objects in nature.
Other mathematical fractals can also be very beautiful. We will explore some of them here.

content.text:
1. Predict first: look at one leaf of a fern. Does it look like a small copy of the whole fern?
2. Each leaf is a smaller fern, and each sub-leaf is a smaller copy again. This is self-similarity.
3. Trees, clouds, coastlines and lightning repeat the same pattern at smaller scales. Can a rule in mathematics make a shape like this, one step at a time?

concepts.concept_name: Building the carpet step by step

content.text:
The Polish mathematician Sierpinski discovered a type of fractal known as the Sierpinski Carpet. It is made by taking a square, breaking it into 9 smaller squares, and then removing the central square; the same procedure is then repeated on the remaining 8 squares, and so on. One then sees the same pattern at smaller and smaller scales.
Draw the initial few steps (at least till Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Carpet.
By its construction, each step in the sequence has (i) squares of the same size that remain in the figure, and the size of these squares becomes smaller and smaller as the step number increases, and (ii) square holes that are formed by removing square pieces.
Do you see any pattern in the number of holes and squares that remain at each step?

content.text:
1. Predict first: Step 1 leaves 8 squares. How many small squares remain after Step 2?
2. At Step 1 the square is split into a 3 by 3 grid and the centre is removed: 8 squares remain, 1 hole.
3. At Step 2 each of the 8 squares is split into 9 and loses its centre: 8 × 8 = 64 squares remain.
4. The 8 new centres are new holes, and the first hole is still there, so there are 1 + 8 = 9 holes.

content.text:
Worked example: Draw Steps 0, 1 and 2 of the Sierpinski Carpet and count the remaining squares and the holes at each step.
1. Step 0: one whole square, no hole.
2. Step 1: a 3 by 3 grid with the centre removed leaves 8 squares and 1 hole.
3. Step 2: each of the 8 squares loses its own centre, so 8 × 8 = 64 squares remain.
4. Holes at Step 2: the old hole plus 8 new ones, 1 + 8 = 9.
Answer: Remaining squares 1, 8, 64; holes 0, 1, 9

content.text:
Let Rn represent the number of remaining squares at the nth step, and Hn represent the number of holes at the nth step.
Every square that remains at a given step, say Step n, gives rise to 8 squares that remain at the (n + 1)th step. Thus, we have R(n + 1) = 8 Rn.
Can this be used to get a formula for Rn?
We have R0 = 1, R1 = 8 × 1 = 8, R2 = 8 × 8 = 8². In general, Rn is 8 to the power n.

concepts.concept_name: Holes: old holes plus one for every square

content.text:
Similarly, how do we find the number of holes at a given step?
Every square that remains at the nth step gives rise to a hole in the (n + 1)th step. All the holes present at the nth step remain in the (n + 1)th step as well. Thus, H(n + 1) = Hn + Rn.
So we have R0 = 1, H0 = 0; R1 = 8, H1 = 1; R2 = 8², H2 = 1 + 8; R3 = 8³, H3 = 1 + 8 + 8².

content.text:
Sierpinski came up with another fractal made in a similar way. An equilateral triangle is broken up into 4 identical equilateral triangles by joining the midpoints of the bigger triangle, and then the central triangle is removed. This procedure is repeated on the 3 remaining triangles, and so on.
Show that by joining the midpoints of an equilateral triangle, we divide it into 4 identical equilateral triangles. [Hint: Note that the corner triangles are isosceles.]
This fractal is called the Sierpinski Triangle/Gasket.

content.text:
Figure it Out (sierpinski fractals, question 2): Find the number of holes, and the triangles that remain at each step of the shape sequence that leads to the Sierpinski Triangle.
1. Each remaining triangle gives 3 remaining triangles at the next step: 1, 3, 9, 27, so the count at Step n is 3 to the power n.
2. Each remaining triangle also makes one new hole, and the old holes stay.
3. Holes: 0, 1, 1 + 3 = 4, 1 + 3 + 9 = 13, and so on.
4. At Step n the holes are 1 + 3 + 9 + ... up to 3 to the power (n − 1), which equals (3 to the power n, minus 1) divided by 2.
Answer: Remaining triangles: 3 to the power n. Holes: 1 + 3 + 9 + ... up to n terms, which is (3 to the power n, minus 1) divided by 2

concepts.concept_name: The bump rule of the Koch Snowflake

content.text:
The Koch Snowflake is another fractal, named after the Swedish mathematician Von Koch, who first described it in 1904. We have already encountered this fractal in Grade 6, Ganita Prakash.
To generate it, we start with an equilateral triangle. Each side is (i) divided into 3 equal parts, and (ii) an equilateral triangle is raised over the middle part, and then the middle part is removed.
Effectively, each side gets replaced by a 'bump' shaped structure.
This procedure is repeated on the sides of the new resulting shape, and so on.

content.text:
1. Predict first: a triangle has 3 sides. After every side gets a bump, how many sides are there?
2. One side becomes 4 shorter sides: the two outer thirds and the two sides of the bump.
3. So 3 sides become 3 × 4 = 12 sides, each one third of the old length.
4. The perimeter changes from 3 to 12 × 1/3 = 4 when each starting side is 1 unit.

content.text:
Worked example: Start with an equilateral triangle of side 1 unit. Find the number of sides, the length of each side and the perimeter at Step 1 of the Koch Snowflake.
1. Each side is cut into 3 parts of 1/3 unit, and the middle part is replaced by two sides of a bump.
2. So each side becomes 4 sides: 3 × 4 = 12 sides.
3. Each side is 1/3 unit long.
4. Perimeter = 12 × 1/3 = 4 units.
Answer: 12 sides, each 1/3 unit, perimeter 4 units

concepts.concept_name: Fractals in temples, blankets and prints

content.text:
Fractals have also long been used in human-made art! Perhaps the oldest such fractals appear in the temples of India. An example occurs in the Kandariya Mahadev Temple in Khajuraho, Madhya Pradesh which was completed in around 1025 C.E.; there one sees a tall temple structure, which is made up of smaller copies of the full structure, on which there are even smaller copies of the same structure, and so on. Fractal-like patterns also occur in temples in Madurai, Hampi, Rameswaram, Varanasi, among many others.
Fractals are also common in traditional African cultures. For example, patterns on Nigerian Fulani wedding blankets often exhibit fractal structures.
In the blanket shown in the figure, there are diamond shaped patterns, inside of which there are smaller diamond shaped patterns, and so on.
The modern maestro of fractal art is undoubtedly the Dutch artist M.C. Escher. One famous example involving fractals is his work 'Smaller and Smaller', which exhibits the identical pattern of lizards but at smaller and smaller scales.

1. Predict first: a diamond is drawn inside a bigger one by joining the midpoints of its sides. Does the inner diamond take more or less than half the area?
2. Joining the midpoints of a rhombus gives a shape with exactly half its area, because each corner cut off matches a piece left inside.
3. Repeating it gives a diamond pattern like the Fulani blankets, each shape half the one before.
4. The temple spire is built of smaller spires in the same way; Escher's lizards shrink ring by ring.

content.text:
Worked example: A diamond pattern has area 64 square cm. Each new shape is drawn by joining the midpoints of the sides of the one before. What is the area of the third shape inside?
1. Joining the midpoints keeps exactly half the area each time.
2. First shape inside: 64 ÷ 2 = 32 square cm.
3. Second: 32 ÷ 2 = 16 square cm.
4. Third: 16 ÷ 2 = 8 square cm.
Answer: 8 square cm

Figure it Out (koch snowflake, question 1): Draw the initial few steps (at least till Step 2) of the shape sequence that leads to the Koch Snowflake.

content.text:
Figure it Out (koch snowflake, question 2): Find the number of sides in the nth step of the shape sequence that leads to the Koch Snowflake.
1. Step 0 has 3 sides.
2. Each step turns every side into 4 sides, so the count is multiplied by 4.
3. Step 1: 3 × 4 = 12. Step 2: 12 × 4 = 48. Step 3: 48 × 4 = 192.
Answer: 3 × (4 to the power n) sides at Step n

Answer: 3 × (4/3) to the power n units; the perimeter keeps growing

1. Predict first: close your eyes and cut the four corners of a square from midpoint to midpoint. What shape is left, and is it bigger or smaller than the four corners put together?
2. The four cuts are equal and meet at right angles, so a smaller square is left, standing on a corner.
3. Each corner is a right triangle; turn the four triangles so their right angles meet at the centre and they form another square.
4. The two squares have the same area, each half of the starting square.

content.text:
Worked example: A square has side 4 cm. Its corners are cut off from midpoint to midpoint. Find the area of the square that is left and of the square made from the four corners.
1. The starting square has area 4 × 4 = 16 square cm.
2. Each corner triangle has two sides of 2 cm at a right angle: area 2 × 2 ÷ 2 = 2 square cm.
3. The four corners together: 4 × 2 = 8 square cm, and they fit together into a square.
4. The square left over: 16 − 8 = 8 square cm.
Answer: Both squares have area 8 square cm, half of the starting square

content.text:
Worked example: Cut the corners at the thirds of an equilateral triangle of side 9 cm and of a square of side 9 cm. Find the side lengths of the shapes left.
1. Triangle: each side keeps its middle third of 9 ÷ 3 = 3 cm.
2. Each cut corner is an equilateral triangle of side 3 cm, so each cut edge is 3 cm: a regular hexagon of side 3 cm.
3. Square: each side keeps its middle third of 3 cm.
4. Each cut edge is the slanted side of a right triangle with sides 3 cm and 3 cm: √(3² + 3²) = √18, about 4.24 cm.
5. So the octagon has sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, and it is not regular.
Answer: A regular hexagon of side 3 cm; an octagon with sides 3 cm and about 4.24 cm, not regular

content.text:
Making Solids
Many basic solid shapes such as a cuboid, parallelopiped, cylinder, cone, prism, and pyramid can be made using foldable flat materials like paper, cardboard, and even metallic sheets! This is one of the methods for manufacturing hollow solids.
While discussing solids that contain plane surfaces in their boundaries, the notion of faces, edges and vertices serves a useful purpose.
Faces are the plane/flat surfaces of a solid that form its boundary. Edges are the line segments that form the sides of the faces, and vertices are the points at which the edges meet. For example, a cuboid or cube has 6 faces, 12 edges and 8 vertices.

content.text:
There are multiple types of prisms and pyramids, whose names depend on the shapes of their faces.
Prism: A prism, in general, has two congruent polygons as opposite faces, with edges connecting the corresponding vertices of these polygons. All the other faces are parallelograms. Based on the shape of the congruent polygons, prisms may be called triangular prisms, pentagonal prisms, and so on.
If the congruent polygons of a prism have 10 sides, how many faces, edges and vertices does the prism have? What if the polygons have n sides?

content.text:
Worked example: A gift box is a prism on an octagon, and its lid is a pyramid on the same octagon. Find the faces, edges and vertices of each.
1. Prism, n = 8: faces 8 + 2 = 10, edges 3 × 8 = 24, vertices 2 × 8 = 16.
2. Pyramid, n = 8: faces 8 + 1 = 9, edges 2 × 8 = 16, vertices 8 + 1 = 9.
3. Check the prism: faces + vertices − edges = 10 + 16 − 24 = 2.
4. Check the pyramid: 9 + 9 − 16 = 2.
Answer: Octagonal prism: 10 faces, 24 edges, 16 vertices; octagonal pyramid: 9 faces, 16 edges, 9 vertices

Check the prism: faces + vertices − edges = 10 + 16 − 24 = 2.
Check the pyramid: 9 + 9 − 16 = 2.
content.answer: Octagonal prism: 10 faces, 24 edges, 16 vertices; octagonal pyramid: 9 faces, 16 edges, 9 vertices
